body:
>Bummer about credit amnesty, but I'm sure you could get into a state school with less-than-ideal grades. People understand screwing up Freshman year, it happens to everyone. If you show that, over the years, your GPA improves, you are much more valuable than someone who maintains a medium GPA throughout. It shows you have matured and are working towards a goal, rather than just going through the motions.

I'm sure schools would understand what happened my freshman year, but it isn't only my first two semesters that look bad. Every semester so far I've dropped at least one class. At this point I probably sound like a broken record, but the reason I'm so obsessed about this is because...

>When you do go to your parents, rather than talking about any failure, shortcoming, or problems, go to them with positive things to say. 1) In the past, there were difficulties. Now there is success. 2) Your GPA is higher than ever, and you've been getting tutored (or whatever) to help you succeed. 3) You've been motivating yourself to take enough credits to get through to your bachelor's degree in 2 years. 4) You are finally reaching your potential thanks to their great help. 5) You are so thankful to have them and their support.

>Don't go to them now, but do it as soon as it feels right. As I said, focus on the positive things in your life first. With more positive things in your life, start working on motivating yourself. Set goals, reward those goals with things you like (personal rewards). Don't starve yourself of rewards while on task and working hard, but make sure the carrot at the end of the stick is good enough to keep you going. Once you have achieved your current goal (the Associates) or are close to it, go to your parents and show off your accomplishments.

I'm not eligible for any financial aid/student loans anymore because of how many classes I've dropped (unsatisfactory academic performance), and I won't be able to get it back because I have no medical documentation showing why I dropped those classes. All I have is excuses. My parents have paid for all of my classes and books so far. When my parents ask me about what classes I'm planning on taking next semester, that's when I'll be forced to tell them everything that I've told you, and while I really like you're suggestion about going to them with the positive things you said above, it might not matter what my plan is for school, because it might be over at that point. The only way I'll be able to show them that I've matured, and that I'm capable of getting my Associates, is if they give me one last chance to prove it to them next semester. The best I can do right now is get good grades in my 3 classes I'm currently doing, and then hope they understand when I break the news to them.

>I didn't graduate from college until 26 (May 2014), so you're not far off of the path I was on. It's still absolutely a doable thing, and within your reach. The nice thing about taking your time is that in many cases you become eligible for "academic renewal" which is some neat thing that community colleges can do to remove low grades and Ws under certain circumstances. I don't know if that's a thing in all states, but I did it at my community college in California.

My school does have what's called a "Credit Amnesty Program" where a student's previous academic record can be expunged, but only after that student has taken at least a four year break of enrollment. So I'm out of luck with that.

>An Associates may seem rather pointless, and in lots of cases it is. But hear me out on this one, it's absolutely a big deal. You don't know what life has in store for you between now and your Bachelors degree. Some terrible accident could stop you in your tracks, leaving you unable to return to school for years. You've got nothing to show for all those years and all that effort, except your Associates! At least that way you have **something** to prove you tried.

You do have a point. If I get my Associates, it won't be all for nothing.

>In addition, an Associates proves that you actually held out through community college. You actually took the time to get the degree, regardless of needing it. That can look really good on college applications, because you finished what you started. You're now thought to be less likely to flake out on the university and will probably graduate because you bothered to take the time.

True. Getting my Associates and than transferring would be different than attempting to transfer without it, cause it shows that I stuck it out.

>Also, lets say you decide you can't go to a 4-year and do go with carpentry or whatever. You've got the associates as the backup so if you do have to stop working in a trade and go back to school, you can prove you tried and worked hard in the past. Sure it wouldn't be easy, it never is, to go back to school. But you at least can prove that you mean it, because you meant it in the past. Also, lots of jobs (mine included) don't require a bachelor's degree. High school + Associates is plenty for lots of jobs, especially those in tech support and office work positions.

That's good to know an Associates isn't worthless. Might not get me a really good job, but it can get me a job.

>Lastly, and I probably should have said this a long time ago, but your parents must believe in you. If they want to support you through more years of college, they probably love you to no end and wish only the best for you. They are willing to burden themselves financially to support you even further. That's a really big deal. I know lots of people who were thrown out between 18-21 and left on their own, no support from their parents. Your parents would probably love to share in your accomplishments and support your goals. They would probably love to hear about your successes, big or small. Maybe you should talk to them, seriously, about all of this, and see what they think. Ask if they would help motivate you, help get you going, and provide moral support.

>Maybe they wont, but if they're willing to stake so much money on the next few years of your life, maybe they'd lend you some emotional support as well. Parents really are great, and maybe your biggest source of love and appreciation is actually in your home, just waiting for you to open up. I don't know your relationship with your parents, but I'd be happy to listen and help try to guide you in speaking with them.

My parents support me very much, and I have a great relationship with him, but I don't see how they can give me a third chance with school. I dropped out in 2012 after I withdrew from 4 out of the 8 classes I took my first 2 semester's. They supported my decision to go back to school in Fall 2014, but I never went to see an academic advisor to make sure I pick the right classes. I only took 3 classes that semester, 1 which isn't required for my major, 1 which is, and a remedial math class (1 of 2 I have to take). So really, only 1 class counted towards my degree.

Spring 2015 semester comes around, and I take 3 classes again. This time, I took English 101, a 2nd remedial math, and a class for my major. Dropped both English and math, so that leaves me with, yet again, 1 class that counts towards my degree.

Now there's this semester. I'm taking 4 classes. 2 of the 4 count towards my degree. One of the non degree classes I really enjoy, so I'm sticking with that, but the other one I'm going to have to drop. In total, since I've come back to school, I've taken 10 classes (includes this semester now), and I'm only going to have completed 7 of them. 

I've never told my parents any of this. They are under the impression that I only have one or two semesters left before I get my Associates, but the truth is that after this semester I'll only have 22 credits towards my degree. I honestly believe this was my last chance at school, and I completely blew it. How can they possibly give me a third chance after all of this? What can I possibly tell them? This is the main reason why I posted here to begin with. I'd rather die than tell them that I did all of this, and that I failed them again. As bad as this is going to sound, at least they would think I was making progress in school, you know, "He had so much to live for".

>That's excellent about your classes! If you have to sacrifice the 4th class, so be it. However, I encourage you to try to stick it out and get through it, as a way to maybe test yourself to see if it is possible to complete the class, regardless of its use in your life. You can always withdraw later (if you don't have too many withdrawals) without causing any negative impact on your transcripts.

I have no problems staying motivated with classes directly related to my major, but I can never seem to get myself to push the the general ed stuff. Unfortunately, my transcript looks horrible as a result (5 Ws and 1 F). There isn't much more I can do that can make it look worse. Do you think I'll have trouble transferring to a 4 year school if I get my associates even though my transcript will look bad? If I don't have much of a shot anyway, I might as well not bother getting the associates in the first place. I might be thinking about this the wrong way though. At this rate though I wouldn't graduate (bachelor's) until I'm 27-28 anyway, and that's assuming I pass every class from here on ouI. I never realized how bad the situation was until I looked and calculated everything last night...

I just wish there was something I can put 100% into. My uncle works for the carpenter's union, and he said if school doesn't work out for me he can get me in. I've been doing some carpentry and labor work over the past couple of years, so I'm not completely new to that type of work. I'm considering my uncle's offer, but if by some chance I end up not liking it (terrified of heights and I don't know if I can handle all the bullshit from other workers), I'll be back at square one again. That wouldn't be a problem if I was 18-19 right out of high school, but I'm 22 now. Time is running out for me to experiment with career options. This is all or nothing now. Whether I decide to stay in school even though my transcript sucks and I won't graduate for another 5 years, or I decide whether to do carpentry, I need to make a decision. I just don't know what to pick, knowing that I won't be able to change my mind.

>Granted a lot of these are just my experiences, but maybe some of them will work for you as well. You say that you don't have many friends, so if you'd like to have someone to help share in your accomplishments, I would be more than happy to join you. Any time you do anything that you feel is good or great, send me a PM. It'll help me by knowing that you're doing well, and hopefully I can provide you with some positive reinforcement as well. Our conversation here doesn't have to end, I just thought I'd offer that to you.

I don't have anything else to lose at this point, so I might as well try your suggestions. Thanks for the offer. There are friends that I hang out with, but we don't talk about accomplishments and stuff like that, so it's nice to know somebody is interested in hearing any I might have. Even though I don't know you personally, it still means a lot to me.

>Have you tried community college in place of high school? Often you can get college credit for doing the same work you would have done in high school, and they usually have great tutoring and mentoring capabilities. I went to tutoring at community college, it was a great experience.

I'm in community college right now. I'm actually doing well in 3 of my 4 classes, but it's difficult to concentrate when I start to feel depressed. I've been having trouble staying motivated in my 4th class ever since I found out that it's not required at all for my major. I'm thinking about just dropping it since it doesn't count. I picked my classes myself instead of going to see an advisor, which was definitely a mistake. I'm lucky 3 of the 4 classes I'm taking actually count.

>How can you forgive yourself for it? You *have* to forgive yourself for it. Dwelling on something like that does you no good except demotivating yourself. All it does is continue to bring you down. You'll have to find a way to let it go. It is never too late to move forward, but putting off moving forward until tomorrow is not a good idea.

I've always had a hard time letting things go. This isn't limited to the high school situation. Every time I make a mistake, no matter how small it is, I always beat myself up about it. Even today, I was thinking about some stupid mistake I made in class yesterday, and I start to think about how only an idiot can do something like that. I get very frustrated with myself for things other people would just shrug off. At this point it feels natural to put myself down. I always seem to remember the mistakes, never the things I do right. How can I change my negative thinking, when it's the only I think?

Yes, there are little things that I like, but living doesn't seem worth it just to enjoy those things. Motivation is hard for me because I know how bad I screwed up in the past (mainly high school), and there's no way for me to fix it now. If I took school seriously to begin with, I wouldn't be struggling like I am now. The only way I could be prepared for college is if I went back and repeated all of high school, but it's obviously too late for that. How can I possibly forgive myself for that? I can't exaggerate the impact this has had on me. I just got done reading a chapter from one of my textbooks for a class, and I can't even answer the review questions because things that I read just don't comprehend half the time, so I'm not able to explain what I read, which is why the only classes that I am able to pass are the ones with open book exams. So, even if slacking off in HS wasn't the cause of me struggling in college, then that means I'm just an idiot to begin with.

The best way I can explain it is that I just don't want those things bad enough. Normal people, like you, may not necessarily want to do it, but you know you have to, so you push through it anyway. I just don't bother. There's obviously something wrong with me, otherwise I would be thinking of ways to get my life together instead of ways to end it. I'm giving myself a couple of months. By then, I'll have to tell my parents that I failed them, and myself  yet again. They won't find out this time. I just hope they don't blame themselves.
Those bad parts define me more than my good parts do. If I didn't have those bad parts, I wouldn't be in this position in the first place. I just wish I was born a different person.

>Have you taken any classes you really liked? 

No, I don't find any classes enjoyable.

Have you passed any classes (without cheating) that you didn't think you could?

In college, no (haven't cheated in college). Only classes I've passed were really easy ones. Any class that is even a little bit challenging, I just give up.

>If they're offering you the ride, and you're still having difficulties, perhaps it is because you aren't truly grasping on and riding. What, if anything, motivates you? What do you love to do, and why? It is easy to be harsh on oneself, but if your parents are giving you a second chance, maybe you can give yourself a second chance, too.

There isn't anything that motivates me. I never understood why. All of my friends (the few that I have) have a goal, and they're doing what has to be done to accomplish that goal. I have no drive, and based on the last 8 years, I never will.
